cases.task:
Request:
Revise this notice for households on a small water network. Make the sequence and the reason for each instruction easy to follow, while keeping a calm, practical tone. Use only the information supplied. Return the revised notice, not editing advice.

Source:
The storage tank will be isolated on Tuesday between 09:00 and 13:00 so that its inlet valve can be replaced. The two wells will continue feeding the network during the work. That is why we expect water to remain available, although the upper streets may experience lower pressure. The work is being done to stop a leak inside the valve assembly, which has made it harder to control the tank level. This has not affected the water-quality tests taken last week.

Please fill a jug before 09:00 if you need drinking water during that period. We are making this suggestion because a brief interruption is possible when the connections are switched, rather than because we expect the entire four-hour window to be without supply. Please also avoid running sprinklers until the tank is back in service. This is a request to keep demand manageable while the wells are supplying the network directly. It would help if washing machines could wait, too, but essential household use can continue.

After the valve is opened, some taps may briefly run cloudy. Air introduced during the work can cause cloudiness that clears in a glass from the bottom upward. If it does not clear, or if the water is discoloured, stop using that tap for drinking and call the service desk. Last week's tests do not tell us what is coming from an individual tap after the repair, so we still need those reports. We cannot promise that every report will have the same explanation.

A completion notice will be posted on the community board when the tank is in service again. The announced end time is an estimate. Until that notice appears, the request about sprinklers still applies. Residents do not need to keep a tap running while they wait for the work to finish.

assertions.text: Preserves Tuesday, the 09:00–13:00 estimated work window, continued well supply, and the possibility of lower pressure or a brief switching interruption.
Keeps last week’s water-quality results distinct from the condition of water at a tap after the repair, without promising present safety or inventing a general boil-water instruction.

Retains the distinction between cloudiness that clears from the bottom upward and persistent cloudiness or discolouration, with stopping drinking use of that tap and contacting the service desk required for the latter, without adding an unprovided clearing procedure.
Makes the relationship between preparation, the work period, and restoration easy for a resident to follow without flattening the notice into disconnected commands.
Consolidates repeated explanations while retaining the different reasons for storing a jug and reducing discretionary demand.
Connects the end of the sprinkler request to the completion notice rather than treating 13:00 as a guaranteed restoration time.
Uses a calm service voice and preserves the distinction between optional postponement of washing and permitted essential use.

cases.task:
Request:
Rewrite the field-camp update for the volunteer newsletter, using the short sample as a guide to the writer's voice. Preserve the actual observations and the limits of what the team knows. The sample is stylistic context, not additional field evidence. Return only the revised update.

Source:
Voice sample:
We carried the spare stakes all morning and used two. I was glad of the other six anyway. The ridge looks close from camp; by the time you reach it, you have usually revised your opinion of the map.

Draft update:
On the first morning, the team found that the stream crossing marked on the route sheet was under water. The replacement route took forty minutes longer, and that mattered because the moth sheets had to be checked before the sun reached the clearing. We got there after it had reached the eastern sheet, although the other two were still in shade. The notes for that sheet now say late check. This is something we have recorded so that the count does not look directly comparable with the others, which were checked on time.

We counted fewer moths on the eastern sheet. That may have something to do with the late visit, but the sheet is also nearer the exposed edge of the clearing. We cannot decide between those explanations from one morning, or rule out another explanation. It would not be accurate to say the route change reduced the count, even though it certainly made us late. This was a frustrating start, but everyone kept the labels with the samples, which sounds like a small victory until a damp paper bag has lost its pencil mark.

The next two mornings we used the longer route and left earlier. All three sheets were checked in shade. Those mornings do not repair the first count; they give us two mornings with matching timing. We are leaving the first observation in the notebook with its warning attached. The spare bootlaces were used to secure a loose sheet corner, and the repair lasted. For the next visit we need another route sheet with the longer walk marked on it. We also need dry bags, which would have been a useful thing to remember before the rain rather than during it.

assertions.text: Preserves the late eastern-sheet check on the first morning and the on-time shaded checks of all three sheets on the next two mornings.
Does not convert the possible effects of timing or exposure on moth counts into an established cause, and does not invent later counts.
Keeps the first observation with its warning rather than implying it was deleted, repaired, or made comparable by later visits.
Carries over the sample’s concrete, mildly dry first-person field voice without copying its map anecdote into the update.
Reduces repetitive uncertainty language while retaining the substantive uncertainty about the lower count.
Makes clear why route duration mattered for checking conditions and why earlier departures changed the later procedure.
Integrates the practical requests and modest humor naturally, without turning the newsletter into a formal incident report.

cases.task:
Request:
Edit this handover note for the next users of a community telescope. Improve readability and organization without making it sound like a product manual. Keep the writer's useful practical detail and avoid adding equipment specifications or troubleshooting steps.

Source:
The telescope is back in the shed after the open evening. I left the small eyepiece case on the lower shelf because the top shelf is directly below the roof seam. There was no water in the shed last night, but that seam has dripped before. The two eyepieces used at the session are in their labelled slots. The third slot is empty because its eyepiece is away for cleaning, not because anyone has lost it.

The finder bracket was tightened before we packed up. Its alignment still needs checking against the main telescope at the start of the next session. Tightening the bracket stopped the movement we could feel; it did not establish that the finder was pointing at the same object. We used the bright star near the western roofline for the final check, but that sightline will not necessarily be useful at the time of your session.

The battery display showed two bars when we closed the shed. I do not know how much observing time that represents. The extension lead is hanging by the door, and the charger is beside the case. Please return the charger there when you finish so that the next group does not have to search for it in the dark.

One of the visitors suggested leaving the dust cap loose to make it easier to remove. We put it back properly before leaving, as usual. It can feel stiff at first. The note about that is here only because somebody may remember the suggestion and wonder whether we followed it. Finally, the sign-in book is dry, but the loose attendance sheet is still on the indoor drying rack. Please leave it there until the paper is dry enough to handle.

assertions.text: Retains the absent eyepiece’s known cleaning status, the prior roof leak as the reason for shelf placement, and the absence of water last night.
Keeps bracket stability distinct from finder alignment and requires a fresh alignment check without prescribing a new method.
Reports two battery bars without inventing a runtime estimate and preserves the charger’s return location.
Organizes the note so equipment readiness and items that need attention can be found easily while preserving an informal handover voice.
Trims explanations only where their function is retained, including the reason for mentioning the dust-cap suggestion.
Keeps the attendance sheet’s drying instruction distinct from the already dry sign-in book.

cases.task:
Request:
Revise this reply from a repair cooperative to a household deciding whether to book a second dishwasher visit. Make the explanation and available choice clear, retaining a candid, non-sales tone. Do not add a diagnosis, price, or promise.

Source:
At the first visit we replaced the split inlet hose and ran a short cycle. No water appeared beneath the machine during that cycle. You have since reported a puddle after a full wash. Those two observations do not conflict, although I can see why the first result made you expect the problem to be finished. A short test without a leak is a result about that test, and we should have explained that more clearly before leaving.

The photograph you sent shows water near the front left foot. It does not show where the water started. It might have travelled along the base before becoming visible. I have put the photograph with the job notes so that the next technician can use it, but it would be premature to name another part for replacement on that basis. The old hose was visibly split and needed replacing. That remains true even though it may not have been the only source of water.

We can offer a second visit to observe a full cycle. There will be no additional call-out charge; any further parts or work would be quoted before you decide. This does not mean that any repair found necessary is included in the first bill. It means the cost of coming out again is waived. If you prefer to pause, the original invoice and the notes from the first visit are available for another repairer.

For now, please leave the machine switched off and do not run another cycle to make a video for us. Your description and photograph are enough to arrange the visit. We have not established whether the new puddle comes from the same fault, a second fault, or something outside the machine. The next visit is intended to narrow that down. It is your choice whether we carry it out, and we can send the available appointments if you want to proceed.

assertions.text: Preserves the split-hose replacement and leak-free short test without claiming that the full-wash problem was fixed or that the first repair was unnecessary.
Keeps the photograph’s visible puddle location separate from an unconfirmed leak origin and leaves the possible relationships among faults unresolved.
States that the second call-out is free but additional parts or work require a quote and a decision, without implying free repairs.
Retains the instruction to leave the machine off and not run a cycle to obtain video, plus the option to take records to another repairer.
Combines repeated cautions where possible while keeping the different limits of the short test, photograph, and future visit.
Explains why observing a full cycle is a reasonable next diagnostic step without guaranteeing that it will resolve the fault.
Maintains responsibility for the earlier unclear explanation and a non-pressuring choice for the household.

cases.task:
Request:
Revise this findings passage for a hypothetical repair-service methods report. Give the discussion a clear progression while preserving the distinction between elapsed waiting and completed turnaround. All numerical summaries and definitions are supplied below. Do not fit a survival model, invent follow-up outcomes, or present the arithmetic bounds as confidence intervals. Return the revised passage.

Source:
We began recording turnaround because customers wanted to know how long a repair would take. The first summary gave a mean of seven calendar days. That number was calculated correctly for the jobs that had finished, but it answered a narrower question than the one customers were asking. At the audit date, several jobs were still waiting for parts. Leaving them out because their final duration was unknown also left out waiting that had already happened.

Forty jobs entered the workshop during the six-week observation window. We audited every job at the same closing date, so later arrivals had shorter follow-up. Turnaround runs from intake to completion, including days spent waiting for parts. Twenty-four jobs had finished, with completed turnaround times totaling 168 days. The other sixteen were unfinished. Their ages at the audit date totaled 208 days. No job had been withdrawn, and the records contained intake dates for all forty. We did not treat the unfinished jobs as completed at their current ages.

For a summary of waiting already accumulated, the two totals can be added. The forty jobs had accumulated 376 days, or 9.4 days per job. If all eventually finish, their mean final turnaround cannot be below 9.4 days, since finishing the pending jobs cannot undo elapsed time. This is a lower bound, not an estimate that their eventual mean will equal 9.4. The available information gives no finite upper bound on how long those jobs might still take. If some never finish, a finite mean completion time for all forty is not established at all.

The service also reports completion within ten calendar days of intake. Eighteen of the completed jobs met that deadline and six did not. Of the sixteen pending jobs, twelve were already older than ten days; the other four were younger than ten days. Thus eighteen jobs were known to have met the deadline and eighteen were known to have missed it. Only four deadline outcomes remained unresolved. The final deadline fraction for this cohort must lie between 18/40 and 22/40, or 45% and 55%, regardless of how much longer the already-late jobs take.

The report should retain the seven-day completed-job mean with its denominator, but it should not headline that mean as the experience of all arrivals. The accumulated-wait bound and deadline interval answer different questions and should retain their definitions. We have not compared repair types or estimated a parts-supply effect. Continuing the record until the remaining deadline outcomes are known would narrow the deadline interval; it would not necessarily finish every job or settle the mean turnaround.

assertions.text: Preserves forty arrivals, a common audit date with unequal follow-up, twenty-four completed jobs totaling 168 days, and sixteen pending jobs with total age 208 days.
Keeps the seven-day mean conditional on completed jobs and the 9.4-day accumulated-wait mean as a lower bound on eventual all-job mean turnaround if all finish, not an imputed completion time.
Retains eighteen timely completions, six late completions, twelve pending jobs already older than ten days, and four pending jobs younger than ten days.
Explains why the final deadline fraction is bounded by 45% and 55% without presenting this deterministic interval as a confidence interval or a modeled estimate.
Distinguishes the absence of a finite upper bound on completion time from the bounded deadline outcome, including the possibility that some jobs never finish.
Connects the customer question, incomplete follow-up, and complementary summaries in readable research prose without repeating a general warning in place of specific qualifications.
Keeps follow-up as proposed and does not infer a parts-supply effect, repair-type comparison, or unobserved completion outcomes.

cases.task:
Request:
Edit the following manuscript passage about a hypothetical seedling-protection study. Improve the exposition of the result and what can reasonably follow from it. Treat all numerical information as fixed. Do not supply literature references or claim to have reanalysed unavailable plot-level data.

Source:
We tested whether small exclosures would improve seedling survival on a grazed slope. Twelve pairs of nearby plots were established, with one plot in each pair randomly assigned an exclosure and the other left open. Ten seedlings were planted in every plot. This gives a reason to compare treatments, but it does not make each seedling an independently assigned experimental unit. The assignment happened to plots within pairs. This distinction becomes important when considering how much certainty the totals can support.

At the final visit, flood damage made one enclosed plot and two open plots inaccessible. We could not determine whether the seedlings in those plots were alive. Among the plots we could inspect, 55 of 110 enclosed seedlings and 42 of 100 open seedlings survived. Thus observed survival was 50% and 42%, respectively. The eight-percentage-point difference refers to the accessible plots. We have not reported a survival estimate that includes the inaccessible plots, and an inaccessible plot has not been treated as a plot with no surviving seedlings.

The enclosed plots may therefore have benefited from protection, but the available totals do not establish how consistent the difference was across the original pairs. Some pairs no longer had both members observed. The final plot-by-plot counts are not available for this passage, so a paired uncertainty estimate cannot be reconstructed from the totals alone. Random assignment is a property of the original study and does not, by itself, settle the possible consequences of the missing final observations.

We also recorded browsing damage among survivors. Eight of the 55 surviving enclosed seedlings and 16 of the 42 surviving open seedlings had damaged shoots. These observations are compatible with reduced browsing under enclosure, but damage was assessed only in plants that remained alive. They cannot tell us how much of the survival difference was mediated by browsing, because damage to plants that died was not measured. It would be easy to merge the two results into one explanation, but the second measurement does not supply that causal link.

For a repeat visit we propose a protocol for recording flood exposure and locating displaced plot markers. This is a proposed improvement in follow-up, not evidence that flooding explains the missing seedlings or the treatment contrast. The present result should remain useful without being asked to answer those additional questions.

assertions.text: Preserves twelve randomized plot pairs, ten seedlings per plot, and missing final outcomes for one enclosed and two open plots without coding them as deaths.
Keeps 55/110 versus 42/100 and the eight-percentage-point contrast tied to accessible plots, with plots rather than seedlings as assignment units.
Retains browsing counts of 8/55 and 16/42 as measurements among survivors and does not turn them into a mediation estimate or observations on dead seedlings.
Explains the inferential roles of the original randomization, incomplete paired follow-up, and unavailable plot-level counts without portraying them as equivalent limitations.

Keeps the suggested flood/marker protocol separate from claims about seedling mortality or the treatment contrast, while retaining documented flood-related loss of access as the reason those final outcomes were unavailable.
Reduces repeated warnings while retaining the specific qualification attached to each result.
Makes the experimental design, accessible-sample result, and interpretation follow coherently without replacing the passage with an audit list.

cases.task:
Request:
Revise this equipment-study excerpt for readers who understand astronomical imaging but have not seen the test. Keep necessary technical terminology and the distinction between measured performance and proposed practical benefit. This is an invented bench study with exactly the evidence given here; no outside citations are needed.

Source:
The practical concern was whether cooling the camera would improve long exposures enough to justify carrying the cooling battery to the field. We began with a bench comparison of dark frames, which can address the detector background without addressing everything that determines an astronomical image. In particular, the test did not contain stars, a telescope, or a moving sky. The battery question motivated the test, but it was not measured by the test.

We used one camera and collected ten thirty-second dark frames at a measured detector temperature of 15 degrees Celsius, followed by ten at 5 degrees Celsius. Exposure time, gain setting, and the covered optical input were unchanged. The order was fixed, warm then cold. At each temperature we formed a median stack of the ten frames. Across pixels, the median value in that stack was 118 ADU in the warm condition and 104 ADU in the cold condition. A separately measured bias level was 100 ADU in both conditions. Subtracting that common level leaves medians of 18 and 4 ADU. These are background signal summaries, not measurements of read noise.

Using a threshold of 250 ADU on each median stack, 120 pixels exceeded the threshold when warm and 40 when cold. The threshold was applied to the raw stack values, before bias subtraction. We refer to these as threshold-exceeding pixels here; the test does not establish that each one is a permanent detector defect. Separate pairs of zero-exposure frames gave the same read-noise estimate, 3.1 electrons, at both temperatures. No conversion from ADU to electrons for the background summaries is supplied in this passage.

The cooler condition therefore had a lower measured dark-frame background and fewer threshold exceedances in this run. The fixed order means that temperature and time in the run were not independently varied. Repeating the sequence in both orders would help evaluate whether that matters. The present result is still a real contrast between the two recorded conditions, even though assigning all of it to temperature requires more than the design provides.

It would also be premature to report better stellar detection or better field endurance. Those outcomes were not tested. A field comparison could examine detection at matched exposure settings while logging battery use. That proposed comparison follows from the original practical concern, which the bench result narrows without settling.

assertions.text: Preserves the single-camera, fixed warm-then-cold order, ten thirty-second frames per temperature, and the 15-degree and 5-degree detector temperatures.
Maintains the distinction between median dark-background summaries in ADU and the separate 3.1-electron read-noise estimates, without inventing a gain conversion.
Keeps the 250-ADU threshold attached to raw median stacks and the 120-versus-40 counts distinct from proven permanent defects.
Relates the bench evidence to the field-use motivation without claiming improved stellar detection, battery endurance, or a fully isolated temperature effect.
Retains legitimate imaging terminology and explains its role without replacing precise terms with misleading everyday synonyms.
Integrates limitations near the claims they restrict instead of repeatedly restarting the discussion.
Presents reordered runs and the field comparison as proposed tests whose different purposes remain clear.

cases.task:
Request:
Revise the draft discussion for a hypothetical document-service evaluation. Build a coherent argument that explains how the reported comparisons can all be correct while answering different questions. Use the synthetic voice sample only as a guide to tone. All evidence and the illustrative weighting calculation are supplied; do not invent tests, user feedback, randomization, or a preferred workload. Return the revised discussion.

Source:
Voice sample:
A fast reply is useful when it reaches the question that was asked. We first counted replies because the system could count them for us. Reading the replies would have answered another question, and we had not yet done that work.

Draft discussion:
We compared two routing methods for requests to a technical document service. Method A sends each request directly to a topic desk. Method B uses a shared intake team before assigning it. The practical question was whether shared intake could help the service respond promptly without using more staff time per request. Both methods operated during the same month, and each request went through only one method. This was a description of the service as operated, not a randomized comparison.

At intake, requests were classified as routine or complex using the same written rule, before their routing method was selected. Supervisors chose the route according to staff availability and the desks involved. Method A received 100 routine requests and 60 complex ones. Method B received 20 routine requests and 80 complex ones. The categories do not measure every difficulty a request can present. We have no finer difficulty scores, and requests within a category should not be assumed interchangeable merely because they share its name.

The recorded outcome was a substantive reply within two working days of intake. An automatic acknowledgement did not count. Method A met the deadline for 80 of its 100 routine requests and 18 of its 60 complex requests. Method B met it for 18 of its 20 routine requests and 32 of its 80 complex requests. All 260 requests had reached the deadline before the records were closed, and none had a missing deadline outcome. The totals are therefore 98 timely replies from 160 requests for A and 50 from 100 for B, giving 61.25% and 50%.

The pooled result favors A on this descriptive measure, but B has the higher fraction within each recorded category. The routine fractions are 80% for A and 90% for B. The complex fractions are 30% and 40%. This is not an arithmetic contradiction. The pooled fractions use different weights: routine work accounts for 100/160 of A's requests and 20/100 of B's. Combining the two category fractions using those different mixtures can reverse their overall ordering. Neither the totals nor the category results should be silently discarded to make the account tell only one story.

As an illustration, applying equal weights to the routine and complex fractions gives 55% for A and 65% for B. Those figures are calculated summaries for a hypothetical half-routine, half-complex mixture. They are not outcomes observed in two additional groups, and equal weighting was not selected because it matched a forecast of next month's workload. The illustration shows the consequence of holding the mixture fixed. It does not establish what would happen if requests were reassigned, since routing was chosen and unrecorded difficulty may still differ within the categories.

Staff logged 48 hours of handling time for A and 35 for B. Dividing by their respective request counts gives 18 and 21 minutes per request. Handling time includes intake and desk work but excludes time waiting for a reply from the requester. It was not broken down by complexity. We therefore cannot combine category-specific deadline rates with category-specific costs, or claim that B requires three extra minutes for an otherwise identical request. The recorded averages describe the two actual workloads.

No one independently assessed whether the substantive replies were correct or sufficient for the requester. Meeting the deadline is a service outcome, but it is not a quality audit. The records also do not identify repeat requesters, so requests cannot be renamed as distinct people served. For the next evaluation we propose recording handling time by complexity and examining reply quality separately. The current comparison should present pooled performance, category performance, and the different workload mixtures together. It does not select a universally preferable routing method.

assertions.text: Preserves the mutually exclusive routing groups, category counts and timely-reply counts, complete deadline follow-up, and the two-working-day substantive-reply definition.
Keeps pooled rates of 61.25% for A and 50% for B consistent with routine rates of 80% and 90% and complex rates of 30% and 40%, respectively.
Explains the reversal between pooled and category-specific rankings through the different workload weights without declaring either valid descriptive comparison erroneous.
Presents equal-weight rates of 55% and 65% as an illustrative hypothetical mixture, not new observations, a forecast, or an identified causal effect of reassignment.
Retains supervisor-selected routing and unmeasured within-category difficulty as limits on causal interpretation; classification occurred before routing.
Keeps 48 and 35 handling hours and the corresponding 18 and 21 minutes per request tied to the actual workloads, with no complexity-specific costs or waiting time included.
Keeps requests distinct from people, deadline success distinct from independently assessed reply quality, and the proposed additional evaluation separate from completed work.
Uses a direct, reflective voice and a coherent passage-level argument without importing the voice sample as study evidence or forcing its wording into the discussion.

cases.task:
Request:
Revise this recommendation to an archive's collections committee. Preserve the writer's proposed decision while making the reasons and treatment of the strongest objection convincing. Work with the stated estimates and uncertainties; do not invent demand data or new funding. Return a complete revised recommendation.

Source:
I recommend using the current allocation to rehouse the loose harbour records and to scan a small sample for evaluation, rather than committing this quarter to scanning the whole group. That recommendation can sound like a preference for work visitors cannot see. Rehousing is largely invisible, and the committee has good reason to want an improvement that people can actually use. It is also true that an image service could reduce the need to handle originals for some requests. Neither point makes the sequence of work unimportant.

The group contains folded sheets whose edges are catching on the existing wrappers. Staff have recorded this condition in the survey. The digitisation estimate assumes the sheets are flattened and stable enough to place safely on the imaging support. It does not include the time needed to bring them to that condition. The rehousing estimate includes sorting out the wrappers and referring the most fragile sheets to the conservator; it does not include treatment of every fragile sheet. We should not let either estimate imply that the difficult preparation is free.

The access argument deserves a better answer than saying the group receives few requests. The catalogue describes it in one broad entry. Low recorded use may partly reflect difficulty finding material, and a useful online sample might reveal interest we have not recorded. We cannot tell from the request count alone whether a full scanning programme would be little used. Equally, potential hidden demand is not yet a measured queue of users waiting for every sheet.

A sample made from sheets cleared for imaging would let us test descriptions and image presentation while rehousing proceeds. It would not estimate the preparation time for the most fragile sheets, because those would be excluded. I propose that the committee ask for a revised full-project estimate after the sample and the condition review. This leaves the eventual digitisation decision open. The immediate choice is to fund work needed for safe access and obtain better information about the larger project. Calling that a delay is fair in calendar terms, but it should not obscure what the intervening work would accomplish.

assertions.text: Preserves the immediate recommendation for rehousing plus a limited cleared-sheet scan sample, with the full digitisation decision deferred rather than rejected.
Keeps the different omissions in the digitisation and rehousing estimates, without representing either as covering all conservation preparation or treatment.
Retains the sample’s exclusion of fragile sheets and the resulting inability to estimate their preparation time from that sample.
Answers the strongest access objection substantively, recognizing that low requests under a broad catalogue entry need not show low underlying demand.
Explains why preparation and the sample support the recommended sequence without treating unmeasured demand as demonstrated or invisible work as automatically superior.
Creates a continuous recommendation with reasons and an intelligible decision point, rather than a series of rebuttal fragments.
Keeps the writer’s candid acknowledgement of calendar delay and the committee’s legitimate interest in visible access improvements.

cases.task:
Request:
Edit this short position statement for discussion at a repair cooperative. Keep its advocacy and informal seriousness, but strengthen the reasoning where the draft jumps between practical and fairness concerns. Do not add evidence that the proposed scheme already works.

Source:
We should try a loan pool for households waiting for a washing-machine repair. At present, the workshop can diagnose a machine quickly and still leave its owner waiting for a part. The gap between those two events is the problem the pool would address. It would not shorten the supplier's delivery time, and it should not be advertised as doing so. I want us to test whether we can make the wait more manageable without making promises the workshop cannot keep.

Six refurbished machines are available for a twelve-week trial. Transport insurance for the trial has already been approved. We have not yet costed the staff time for delivery, collection, and cleaning between loans. That is a reason to keep the trial small and record that time. It is not a reason to pretend the machines are free simply because we already own them. A loan would also be a poor answer for a household where the available machine cannot fit the space or connect safely. Eligibility cannot guarantee suitability.

I favour making the pool open to all customers with a repair booked, while offering delivery-fee assistance according to need. A universal opening rule would avoid asking people to establish hardship before they can even ask about a loan. Fee assistance would still require a separate conversation. These are two different decisions, and combining them into a single test would make the first harder than it needs to be. If demand exceeds six machines, we would need an allocation rule agreed before launch; this statement does not settle that rule.

The older loan machines may cost more to run than some of the machines being repaired. That objection is real, especially for people already struggling with bills. A short loan is a possible bridge, not proof that running costs do not matter. We should explain the known running information for each available machine and let the household decide. At the end of twelve weeks, the cooperative should review actual use, staff time, and reported difficulties before deciding whether to continue. We do not have those results yet.

assertions.text: Keeps the six-machine, twelve-week proposal and approved transport insurance separate from uncosted staff work and unknown trial outcomes.
Preserves open eligibility for customers with booked repairs, need-based delivery assistance, and an allocation rule still to be agreed if demand exceeds supply.
Does not promise shorter parts delays, universal physical suitability, lower running costs, or successful performance of the scheme.
Connects the repair-wait problem to the loan proposal and explains why a bounded trial is justified despite unresolved costs.
Makes the fairness rationale for separating access eligibility from fee assistance understandable while retaining the genuine administrative and capacity limits.
Preserves clear advocacy and the conversational cooperative voice without inflating the proposal into a general solution to appliance access.
Treats higher running costs as a substantive objection requiring information and choice, not an objection dismissed merely because the loan is temporary.

cases.task:
Request:
Revise this opinion piece for a water cooperative's member bulletin. Preserve the recommendation and the competing fairness principle, making the numerical example and the argument easier to follow. All figures are hypothetical annual figures. Do not introduce a legal requirement, predicted demand response, or information about members' incomes.

Source:
The cooperative has a one-off surplus of £1,200 to return across 100 household accounts. I favour a £12 credit on each account. The alternative under discussion is to reduce the volumetric charge on this year's total of 20,000 cubic metres, which would give a reduction of £0.06 per cubic metre. Both approaches return the same £1,200 on the stated figures. The fact that they add to the same total does not mean they answer the same question about fairness.

A household using 40 cubic metres would receive £2.40 under the volumetric reduction. One using 300 would receive £18. Under the equal-credit approach both would receive £12. That difference is why I prefer the credit. It gives each account an equal share of a surplus earned by a member-owned service, and it leaves the price of an additional cubic metre unchanged. It does not mean every household would see the same percentage reduction in its bill. Their bills and water use differ.

The strongest case for the volumetric option is that people who bought more water paid more in volume charges, so returning money in proportion to purchases looks like a refund. That is a reasonable principle. My preference rests on treating this particular surplus as a common benefit rather than as the correction of an identified overcharge. The surplus has not been traced to an error on any account. We should say which principle we choose instead of making the other one sound arithmetically confused.

Equal credits are not the same as targeted help. We do not have income or household-size information in this proposal. A low-use account is not necessarily a low-income household, and a high-use account may serve more people. I am not claiming that a £12 credit reaches those in greatest need. Nor have we estimated whether a temporary volume-price reduction would change use. Keeping the marginal price unchanged preserves the current price schedule; it does not demonstrate a conservation effect. The case for the credit is modest but sufficient: equal treatment of accounts for a one-off common surplus, without revising the usage rate to accomplish it.

assertions.text: Preserves the £1,200 surplus, 100 accounts, 20,000 cubic metres, £12 equal credit, and £0.06 volume reduction, with correct £2.40 and £18 example refunds.
Retains the equal-credit recommendation as a one-off decision and does not turn it into an ongoing tariff change or an identified-overcharge correction.
Keeps account equality distinct from percentage bill equality, household need, and household size, without inventing demographic information.
Explains both common-benefit and purchase-proportional refund principles fairly and locates the preference in a normative choice rather than an arithmetic advantage.
Keeps unchanged marginal price distinct from an empirically demonstrated reduction in consumption.
Integrates the examples into the reasoning so the arithmetic advances the comparison instead of interrupting it.
Reduces repeated defensive phrasing without dropping the material limits on distributional or conservation claims.

cases.task:
Request:
Revise this fieldwork planning note into a clear argument for the stated scheduling proposal. Keep the disagreement respectful and preserve the practical constraints. Do not resolve the debate by inventing extra volunteers, funding, or evidence about animal behaviour.

Source:
I propose that we alternate which six of the eight shoreline sectors we survey on each visit, using the same observation protocol in every sector we reach. Our present daylight window allows six sectors at the required pace. Trying to fit eight into it has led to rushed notes at the last stops. That is recorded in the visit logs. We should stop writing a schedule which only works if the final sectors receive a different kind of visit from the first ones.

There is a serious objection. The coordinator wants every sector covered on every visit because a missed sector can contain a short-lived nesting event. Alternating coverage would create planned gaps, and the logs cannot tell us how many events those gaps would miss. The rushed visits are still visits, and it would be wrong to pretend they provide no information. The choice is between different losses, not between a complete record and an empty one.

One suggestion is to split the team into pairs and run two routes. We already work in pairs under the group's shoreline safety protocol, and only two trained observers are available on these visits. Splitting those two would change that protocol. Adding a second pair could change the scheduling calculation, but there is no second trained pair available for the coming month. It is a useful future option rather than an answer to the next four visits.

For those four visits, I suggest publishing the rotation in advance and marking unvisited sectors explicitly in the record. The rotation should give each sector three visits across the month. This is feasible because four visits with six sectors each provide twenty-four sector visits in total. A planned absence would then be distinguishable from a visit on which no nest was recorded. It would still be an absence. At the end of the month we could review whether the notes were more complete and whether additional staffing had become possible. That review would not recover events missed during gaps, but it would let us reconsider the schedule with a clearer account of what we had done.

assertions.text: Preserves eight sectors, capacity for six per visit, four upcoming visits, and the proposal for three visits per sector across that month.
Keeps the two-observer paired safety constraint and the absence of a second trained pair, without inventing staffing or authorizing solo routes.
Maintains the distinction between unvisited sectors and visited sectors with no recorded nest, and does not claim that later review recovers missed events.
Acknowledges the genuine risk of missing short-lived events and the information retained by rushed visits instead of portraying the alternative as worthless.
Uses the feasible scheduling totals to support a rotation while preserving that the proposal trades forms of information loss rather than eliminating loss.
Makes the operational constraint, objection, and bounded proposal progress clearly without manufacturing a consensus.
Keeps the tone respectful and practical, with the documented rushed notes distinguished from unmeasured effects on event detection.

cases.task:
Request:
Rewrite this mathematical passage for an equipment scheduling appendix. Preserve the exact return period, reachable-slot description, and edge cases, while making the compressed divisibility argument readable. The schedule is an idealized model, not a measured hardware property. You may use the elementary fact that coprime integers u,v admit integers a,b with au+bv=1.

Source:
A recorder has n labeled memory slots, numbered 0 through n−1, where n is a positive integer. Starting at slot a, with 0 ≤ a < n, it advances by a fixed integer s ≥ 0 after every write. Write x_k for the residue of a+ks modulo n, with k ≥ 0. A return means x_k=a for a positive k, not merely that two numerical representatives look similar. Let g=gcd(n,s), taking gcd(n,0)=n. We claim that the least positive return time is n/g, and that the visited slots are exactly those congruent to a modulo g. There are g disjoint cycles across all starting slots.

Put n=gn' and s=gs', so gcd(n',s')=1. A return after k steps occurs exactly when n divides ks, or equivalently when n' divides ks'. Coprimality implies that n' then divides k. To justify that implication, choose integers u,v with un'+vs'=1 and multiply by k. Both terms on the left are divisible by n' when n' divides ks'. Conversely k=n' does give a return. Thus no smaller positive step count works.

The first n' visited residues are distinct: equality at two indices would make their positive difference, less than n', a return step count. Every visited residue is congruent to a modulo g because both s and n are multiples of g. Exactly n/g slots have that congruence, so the distinct visited residues exhaust them. The g congruence classes partition the slots and give the claimed cycles.

When s=0, the return time is one and every cycle is a single slot. When n=1, there is only slot zero regardless of s. No step in the argument divides by s, assumes that s<n, or treats rotations of the labeled slots as a new schedule.

assertions.text: Preserves n as a positive integer, s as a nonnegative integer, labeled residues, and a starting slot in the stated range.
Retains least positive return time n/gcd(n,s), the exact reachable congruence class, and the number of disjoint cycles.
Explains the equivalence of returning and divisibility and justifies cancellation of the coprime factor using the supplied integer identity or equivalent elementary reasoning.
Establishes both that n/g is a return time and that no smaller positive return time is possible.
Justifies distinctness before the first return and exhaustion of the congruence class, rather than only showing that visits remain inside it.
Handles s=0, n=1, and step sizes at least n without division by zero or an added restriction.
Presents a connected proof with intermediate relations made explicit and keeps the mathematical scheduling model separate from claims about physical equipment.

cases.task:
Request:
Revise this finite-probability proof for a methods appendix about paired synthetic labels. Explain the construction and its optimality without adding independence to the coupling being optimized. Preserve zero-probability labels and both boundary cases. Use the supplied finite sums rather than citing a coupling theorem in place of the argument.

Source:
Let p_1,...,p_m and q_1,...,q_m be probability vectors on the same m labeled outcomes, where m ≥ 1. Entries may be zero. A coupling is an array J_ij ≥ 0 whose row sums are p_i and column sums are q_j. It describes two labels U,V on a common probability space, and their agreement probability is Σ_i J_ii. We claim that the largest possible agreement is

Σ_i min(p_i,q_i) = 1 − (1/2)Σ_i |p_i−q_i|.

For any coupling, J_ii cannot exceed either its row sum or its column sum. Adding these bounds gives the upper bound. To attain it, put c_i=min(p_i,q_i), α_i=p_i−c_i, β_i=q_i−c_i, and r=1−Σ_i c_i. Both residual vectors have sum r, and α_iβ_i=0 for every label i. These residuals refer to unused probability mass, not negative observations.

If r>0, define

J_ij = c_i 1{i=j} + α_iβ_j/r.

Summing over j gives c_i+α_i=p_i, and summing over i gives c_j+β_j=q_j. All entries are nonnegative. Its diagonal is exactly c_i because the residual product at the same label is zero. Thus the construction attains the upper bound. The residual product is a device for constructing one joint distribution; it does not say every coupling, or even this entire mixture, has independent coordinates.

If r=0, use only J_ii=p_i=q_i and set the other entries to zero. There is no residual division. Finally |p_i−q_i|=p_i+q_i−2c_i, and summing proves the alternative formula. When the distributions have disjoint supports, every c_i is zero and the largest agreement is zero. Zero entries and a one-label space require no change to the statement. The comparison optimizes how the two labels are paired while keeping each marginal distribution fixed; it does not change either probability vector.

assertions.text: Preserves finite labeled probability vectors with possible zero entries, fixed marginals, and optimization over all nonnegative coupling arrays.
Retains both equivalent formulas for maximum agreement without assuming independent coordinates.
Justifies the diagonal upper bound from row and column sums and shows why attaining it establishes optimality.
Verifies nonnegativity, both marginals, and the diagonal of the proposed construction using the equal residual totals and α_iβ_i=0.
Handles r=0 without division, disjoint supports, and a one-label space consistently.
Derives the absolute-difference formula by summing the pointwise minimum identity or equivalent explicit algebra.
Connects the upper bound, construction, and boundary cases as a self-contained proof without confusing the residual product with a required independence assumption.

cases.task:
Request:
Edit this counting proof for a synthetic data-checking appendix. Explain why the completion procedure is consistent and why it counts each array exactly once. Preserve arbitrary prescribed row and column parities, all positive dimensions, and the zero-count case. Return a self-contained statement and proof rather than a general coding-theory discussion.

Source:
Let r,c be positive integers. Consider r-by-c arrays whose entries are either zero or one. Prescribe row parities a_1,...,a_r and column parities b_1,...,b_c, each also zero or one. A row has parity a_i when its entry sum is congruent to a_i modulo two; columns are defined in the same way. We count labeled arrays, so permuting rows or columns generally changes the array. We claim that the number is zero if

Σ_i a_i ≢ Σ_j b_j (mod 2),

and otherwise is 2^((r−1)(c−1)).

Necessity follows because adding all row sums and adding all column sums count the same entries. Suppose the parity totals agree. Choose the upper-left (r−1)-by-(c−1) block freely. There are 2^((r−1)(c−1)) choices. For each of the first r−1 rows, its last entry is uniquely determined by the required row parity. For each of the first c−1 columns, its last entry is uniquely determined by the required column parity. These two steps fill disjoint parts of the border.

Only the bottom-right entry remains. Choose it to make the last row have parity a_r. We must still check the last column; it is not an independent free choice. Once every row has its prescribed parity, the parity of the total array sum is Σ_i a_i. The first c−1 columns already have total parity Σ_(j<c) b_j. Subtracting their contribution modulo two and using equality of the prescribed totals shows that the last column has parity b_c.

Every freely chosen block therefore has exactly one valid completion. Conversely, restricting any valid array to that block recovers its free choice, and the same parity requirements force its border. This is a bijection, so the number of block choices is the number of arrays. If r=1 or c=1, the free block has no entries and one choice. The border argument still works with empty sums interpreted as zero, including r=c=1.

assertions.text: Preserves labeled binary arrays, positive integer dimensions, arbitrary binary prescribed parities, and the stated modulo-two compatibility condition.
Retains zero arrays for incompatible totals and exactly 2^((r−1)(c−1)) arrays when compatible.
Establishes necessity by counting the same total entry sum by rows and by columns.
Shows that each chosen interior block uniquely forces the two disjoint border portions and then the final entry.
Checks the remaining column constraint from total parity rather than assuming that the two requirements for the corner automatically agree.
Establishes the bijection in both directions and covers one-row, one-column, and one-entry arrays without counting empty blocks as having zero choices.
Explains the purpose of each completion step in connected prose, with sufficient equations or explicit parity relations to make the consistency argument checkable.

cases.task:
Request:
Repair and rewrite this matrix-perturbation proof for an instrument reconstruction appendix. The source expressly flags an invalid invertibility inference. Replace it using the given norm hypothesis and elementary finite-dimensional linear algebra, preserving both quantitative bounds. Do not assume symmetry, commuting matrices, or a smaller perturbation than stated. Return a self-contained statement and proof.

Source:
Let A be an invertible real d-by-d matrix, with d ≥ 1, and let H be any real d-by-d matrix. All vector norms are Euclidean, and matrix norms are their induced operator norms. Put E=A^(−1)H and δ=||E||, and assume δ<1. We claim that B=A+H is invertible and

||B^(−1)−A^(−1)|| ≤ [δ/(1−δ)] ||A^(−1)||.

For any vector b, let x=A^(−1)b. Once invertibility of B is established, write x_tilde=B^(−1)b. We also claim

||x_tilde−x|| ≤ [δ/(1−δ)] ||x||.

The statements concern a change in the matrix with the same right-hand side. They do not assume a measured true signal or an empirical error distribution.

We have B=A(I+E). The draft says that I+E must be invertible because I is invertible. That inference is invalid without using the perturbation hypothesis. The missing step must establish invertibility and justify the quantitative estimate ||(I+E)^(−1)|| ≤ 1/(1−δ). You may use the fact that an injective linear map from R^d to itself is surjective. No inverse of I+E may be used before its existence is proved.

After that step, the order of the factors matters. Write

B^(−1)=(I+E)^(−1)A^(−1),
B^(−1)−A^(−1)=−(I+E)^(−1)EA^(−1).

The second identity follows from (I+E)^(−1)−I=−(I+E)^(−1)E. Applying submultiplicativity gives the first bound. Also x_tilde=(I+E)^(−1)x, so

x_tilde−x=−(I+E)^(−1)Ex,

which gives the solution bound. If δ=0, then H=0 and both differences vanish. If b=0, both solutions are zero; this case does not require dividing by ||x||. The coefficient δ/(1−δ) in the solution bound is attained when H=−δA with 0<δ<1 and b is nonzero.

assertions.text: Preserves invertible A, arbitrary H, the induced Euclidean operator norm, and δ=||A^(−1)H||<1 without adding symmetry or commutativity.
Retains the inverse-difference and same-right-hand-side solution bounds with coefficient δ/(1−δ).
Repairs the invalid inference by proving invertibility of I+E using the norm hypothesis, and establishes its inverse norm bound without circular use of an unproved inverse.
Keeps the order in B=A(I+E) and B^(−1)=(I+E)^(−1)A^(−1) correct and justifies the inverse-difference identity.
Derives both quantitative estimates from valid norm inequalities and relates the solution perturbation to x rather than assuming x_tilde=x.
Handles δ=0 and b=0 without division by zero and verifies the stated attainment example for positive δ and nonzero b.
Integrates the repaired step into a connected mathematical proof rather than preserving the invalid inference as a valid step.
Explains the role of the perturbation condition and factorization without expanding the result into unsupported empirical calibration claims.

cases.task:
Request:
Give this already reviewed archive-guide passage a light copyedit. Preserve its professional voice and technical distinctions. Change wording only where there is a concrete readability or correctness gain; returning sound passages unchanged is welcome. Return the full passage.

Source:
The photographs are arranged in the order in which the albums reached the archive. Within each album, the original sequence has been retained. This arrangement preserves evidence about how the collection was assembled, even where the date of an individual photograph is uncertain. A chronological search view is available through the catalogue, but it does not change the physical order of the albums.

Descriptions distinguish information written on a photograph from information supplied later. A date transcribed from the reverse appears in the inscription field. A date proposed by the cataloguer appears in the estimated-date field, together with the basis for the estimate. These fields can disagree without either field having been recorded incorrectly. Readers should use the source of each statement when deciding what weight to give it.

The online images are access copies. Some show the full album page, including mounts and handwritten annotations; others show an individual photograph where the page could not be imaged safely. The image description identifies which kind of view is displayed. Absence of an annotation from an individual-image view does not establish that the album page carries no annotation.

Requests to consult the originals are assessed by condition. Digitisation has made more of the collection visible, but it has not made every album safe to open. If a requested page cannot be served, staff can explain the restriction and identify any available access copy. They cannot promise that an existing copy will answer a question about the paper, mounting method, or reverse of the photograph.

assertions.text: Preserves original physical arrangement separately from the chronological catalogue search view.
Keeps transcribed inscriptions distinct from later estimated dates and does not resolve a possible disagreement by treating one field as necessarily erroneous.
Maintains the difference between full-page and individual-image views and the limit on inferring absent annotations from the latter.
Retains condition-based access and the possibility that an access copy cannot answer questions about physical features.
Exercises copyediting restraint on an already coherent passage, accepting unchanged wording where no concrete improvement is needed.
Preserves useful archival terminology and substantive contrasts instead of treating their form as an automatic style defect.

cases.task:
Request:
Lightly edit this equipment-club column for clarity while preserving the writer's personal voice. The editor has explicitly approved the deliberate humor and the conversational asides. There is no requirement to change a passage that already reads well. Return the column, not a critique.

Source:
I bought the smaller mount because I wanted to observe on evenings when carrying the larger one felt like a separate hobby. The new mount is easier to lift, but its counterweight still has to come along. Apparently gravity declined my request for a luggage allowance. I now carry the weight in a separate bag and make two trips from the door.

That arrangement has been useful for short sessions. I can set the tripod down before bringing out the telescope, and I am less tempted to balance everything against the doorframe. It has not made the equipment suitable for every surface. On the soft ground behind the shed, a tripod foot still settles if I do not give it a firm pad. Portability and stability are related decisions, but they are not interchangeable measurements.

I also kept the old hand controller. Its buttons are easy to find with gloves on, and I already know which menu contains the alignment check. A phone interface might suit someone else. For me, replacing a familiar controller would add another thing to learn during the part of the evening when I would rather look through the eyepiece.

These are observations from my own setup, not a comparison test between mounts. I have used the smaller one on five evenings, all in light wind. The useful result so far is that I have gone outside more often. Whether it tracks as well under a heavier telescope or in stronger wind remains a question for another session, with the appropriate equipment and conditions.

assertions.text: Preserves the smaller mount’s easier lifting, the continuing need for its counterweight, and the two-trip arrangement.
Keeps the account limited to five light-wind evenings with the writer’s own setup, without inventing tracking comparisons or performance under heavier loads.
Preserves the old controller as a personal usability preference and leaves other users’ interface preferences open.
Retains the explicitly approved gravity/luggage joke and the writer’s understated conversational asides, without converting them into formal equipment guidance.
Preserves the legitimate distinction between portability and stability and the practical soft-ground observation.
Uses restraint where the source is already clear and does not manufacture changes to demonstrate editing effort.
Keeps more frequent personal use distinct from a controlled demonstration of superior mount performance.

cases.task:
Request:
Check this field-report passage for readability and make only edits you can justify from the text. Its cautions have been reviewed by the field team and should retain their substance. Do not add management recommendations or evidence. Return the full passage; unchanged prose is acceptable where it is already clear.

Source:
We found three active burrows along the accessible section of the dune after the storm. Each had fresh tracks at its entrance on both survey mornings. We use active here to describe that observed sign. We did not enter the burrows or confirm the presence of young, so the count should not be read as a count of breeding pairs.

The northern section was closed because the access path had collapsed. It was not surveyed from another route. The map therefore marks that section as unobserved, rather than showing it with zero burrows. This distinction matters when comparing the map with the survey made before the storm, which covered the full dune. The two maps have different observation footprints.

Within the area covered on both occasions, one previously recorded entrance was no longer visible. Sand covered its mapped location. We cannot determine from the surface record whether the burrow was destroyed, remained occupied beneath the deposit, or had been abandoned before the storm. The timing of the surveys places the change between visits; it does not identify when an animal left or what caused it to leave.

Photographs were taken from the same marked viewpoints where those viewpoints remained accessible. Two images therefore provide a direct view comparison, while the third post-storm image was taken farther inland. Its caption records that change. The photographs support the descriptions of visible surface conditions. They do not extend the burrow count into the closed section or resolve the status of the covered entrance.

assertions.text: Keeps three active burrows defined by fresh tracks on both mornings and does not equate them with confirmed breeding pairs or young.
Preserves the closed northern section as unobserved and the differing footprints of the pre-storm and post-storm surveys.
Retains the unresolved status of the covered entrance and does not infer destruction, abandonment timing, or storm causation from the surface observations.
Maintains two matched photographic viewpoints and one farther-inland viewpoint, with photographs limited to visible conditions.
Preserves distinct cautions tied to activity, spatial coverage, chronology, and photographic comparability instead of compressing them into a vague general disclaimer.
Recognizes the source’s existing coherent progression and accepts unchanged prose when editing would bring no concrete gain.

cases.task:
Request:
Only revise the second paragraph of this appliance-service note to clarify which component each pronoun refers to. Return the full note, keeping the first, third, and fourth paragraphs verbatim. Preserve the sequence and all findings. Do not broaden the task into a general style rewrite or diagnose an additional fault.

Source:
The refrigerator was inspected after a report that its cabinet light stayed off when the door opened. The cooling compartment was at the requested setting during the visit. That observation was recorded separately from the lighting fault. The customer asked us to restore the light and to explain whether the stored shelves would need to be removed for the work.

The technician removed the lamp cover and placed it beside the replacement lamp. It was cracked along one edge, but it was intact. The cracked item was the old cover; the intact item was the replacement lamp. Before fitting it, the technician checked the socket and cleaned its contacts. Here the item being fitted was the replacement lamp, and the contacts belonged to the socket. It then lit when the door switch was released. The cracked cover was kept off the appliance, and a new cover was ordered.

The shelves remained in place throughout the visit. The customer was shown the light working and was told that the ordered cover would require another short appointment. No date was promised because the supplier had not confirmed dispatch. The order reference was added to the service record, and the customer received a copy of that record.

The follow-up visit is for fitting the cover and checking the light again. If the light stops working before then, the customer should contact the workshop rather than remove the lamp or socket. The present note records what was observed and done during this visit; it does not establish how long the replacement lamp will last.

assertions.text: Keeps the first, third, and fourth paragraphs verbatim, as explicitly requested.
Identifies the old lamp cover as cracked, the replacement lamp as intact and fitted, and the cleaned contacts as belonging to the socket.
Preserves removal of the cover, inspection and cleaning before fitting the replacement lamp, successful lighting on release of the door switch, and the cover order.
Repairs the second paragraph’s ambiguous pronouns using clear component references rather than retaining contradictory unsupported referents.
Integrates the clarifying information into the service account without unnecessary repetition of editorial explanations about what each pronoun means.
Does not invent a cooling fault, additional repair, dispatch confirmation, visit date, or lamp-lifetime guarantee.
Respects the limited edit scope rather than smoothing or rephrasing already sound surrounding paragraphs.

cases.task:
Revise this internal transport notice so dispatchers can follow the decision and its exceptions on a first reading. Preserve the practical, matter-of-fact tone and all operational commitments. Return the revised notice, not an editing plan.

Source to revise:
Starting on the first Monday of the autumn timetable, the westbound museum shuttle will leave the library at 18:10 instead of 18:00 on weekdays. The change is being made because the evening class now finishes at 18:00, although it is not a promise to hold the shuttle until every class has finished. The library stop is where the change begins. The earlier stops on the same vehicle's inbound trip keep their present times.

The dispatch trial covered six evenings. On four of them, moving the departure allowed the class passengers to board without delaying arrival at the station beyond 18:32. On the other two, roadworks delayed both the old departure and the trial departure, according to the paired journey estimates. Those estimates came from vehicle logs rather than two shuttles running alongside one another. This does not establish that the later departure has no effect on arrival, which is why it is a trial and why the time will be checked.

A driver who reaches the library early should wait for 18:10. If the class is still inside at 18:10, the driver should leave. This also applies when a member of staff says the class is nearly finished. Dispatch may authorize a hold for a passenger who has already reached the stop and needs boarding assistance; that existing rule is unchanged. It should not be understood to include waiting for someone still in the building.

The station connection leaves at 18:40. We will record missed connections for the first two weeks, including whether the shuttle or the connecting service was late. They will be reviewed on Friday after the second week. The weekend timetable is unchanged. Please replace the weekday library notice before the first affected departure; the station notice can stay because its advertised arrival is still 18:32.

assertions.text: Preserves the weekday library departure change from 18:00 to 18:10, its first-Monday start, and the unchanged inbound and weekend times.
Retains the distinction between leaving when the class is still inside and an authorized hold for someone already at the stop needing boarding assistance.
Keeps the 18:40 connection, the advertised 18:32 arrival, the two-week recording period, its Friday review, and the different notice-replacement instructions.
Explains that four favorable trial evenings and two log-based paired estimates do not establish that the later departure never affects arrival.
Makes the departure rule and its exception easy to follow without scattering them across repetitive warnings.
Resolves the review sentence's ambiguous antecedent and preserves an operational notice rather than turning it into promotional prose.

cases.task:
Edit this explanation for families for clarity and flow. Keep its reassuring but candid voice, and retain the distinctions that affect how the score should be read. Return a complete revised explanation.

Source to revise:
The reading check that came home this week is one piece of information about how your child reads short passages independently. It is not a grade for this term. We use the same scoring rule in every class, but the passages are not the same for every year group. A score of 14 in one year group therefore should not be compared directly with a score of 14 in another.

The sheet shows a raw score and a band. The raw score is the number of questions answered correctly out of 20. The band groups nearby scores so that we can discuss support without making too much of a one-question difference. It is possible for a child's raw score to improve while the band stays the same. A change of band is also possible after a small change near a boundary. Neither situation tells the whole story by itself.

Some children completed the check in two sittings because the fire alarm interrupted the morning session. Their sheets carry a small circle beside the date. The circle records the interruption, not a concern about the child. We have not adjusted these scores, and we will consider the interruption alongside classroom reading before deciding whether a further check is useful.

Teachers will discuss these results during the scheduled meetings next month. You do not need to arrange another meeting simply because a band has stayed the same. If the sheet does not match what you see when your child reads at home, please send the class teacher a short note. Examples of what feels easier or harder are more useful than extra practice-test scores. Children can continue their usual reading at home; we are not asking families to rehearse the questions.

assertions.text: Retains the distinction between a raw score out of 20, a reporting band, and a term grade, including the warning against direct comparisons across year groups.
Preserves the interruption marker's meaning, the lack of score adjustment, and the use of classroom evidence in considering a further check.
Keeps the next-month meeting arrangement and the invitation to send concrete home-reading observations without asking families to rehearse test questions.
Explains both an improved raw score within a band and a small score change across a band boundary without treating either as a definitive change in reading ability.
Uses language accessible to families without replacing the scoring distinctions with an oversimplified assurance.
Preserves the measured reassurance and permits retaining already clear sentences rather than rewarding edits for their own sake.

cases.task:
Revise this studio handover note into clear connected prose for the next editor. Keep the technical terms that help an experienced audio editor, and preserve the sequence-dependent cautions. Do not add troubleshooting steps or settings.

Source to revise:
The interview edit is ready for the dialogue pass, apart from the short answer after the door closes, which is still the original take. I left it that way because the alternate take is cleaner but changes the speaker's answer from a tentative agreement to an unqualified one. The noise is therefore a reason to treat that section carefully, rather than a reason to swap it. Both takes are marked in the session.

There are two room-tone beds. The one labelled corridor belongs under the first exchange only. The quieter one belongs under the later seated interview. It sounds more even when used everywhere, but that makes the move between rooms disappear. This is the one thing I do not want evened out. The transition itself can be softened; the fact that there is a transition should remain audible.

I have bypassed the broadband denoiser on the music bus, where it was only present because the track template included it. The dialogue denoiser is active. Its printed preview is useful for judging pauses but should not be treated as the final dialogue render, since three edits were made after it was printed. They are marked with blue flags. The flags mark edits made after the print, not necessarily faults in those edits.

Please audition the low-level answer on headphones before adjusting the gate. On the monitors, the first consonant can sound like chair noise, and the current gate already clips part of it. The repair is still outstanding. After that, check the room transition in context and make a fresh dialogue print. The existing preview has been left available for comparison. The delivery mix is not ready yet, even though the rough mix has the requested duration. There is no need to change the music balance on the basis of this note.

assertions.text: Keeps the original tentative answer and does not authorize substitution of the semantically stronger alternate take.
Preserves which room-tone bed belongs to each location and the requirement that the move between rooms remain audible even if the transition is softened.
Distinguishes the bypassed music-bus denoiser, the active dialogue denoiser, and the outdated printed dialogue preview with three later edits marked in blue.
Clarifies the referents of the room-tone and preview passages while retaining useful studio terminology.
Connects the outstanding consonant repair, headphone audition, contextual transition check, and fresh print in the requested order without inventing processing settings.
Retains the incomplete delivery status and does not infer mix readiness from duration or recommend a music-balance change.

cases.task:
Rewrite the volunteer coordinator's draft in the voice of the short sample. Make the arrangements and their reasons easy to understand without making the message more formal. The sample is a voice reference only; revise the draft and do not import facts from the sample.

Synthetic voice sample (reference only):
Thanks for staying through the rain. The umbrellas survived; the sign-in sheet did not. Next time we will keep it inside the gate, where it can do its one small job without becoming soup. If you borrowed a pen, keep it until Saturday. We will need both you and the pen.

Source to revise:
For the next repair morning, people who have already done an induction should arrive at 09:15, while new volunteers should arrive at 09:00. I realize that this makes being new look like a punishment consisting of an earlier alarm, which is not the intention. We need fifteen quiet minutes to show new people the shutoff switches before the room fills up. Returning volunteers can help by not arriving early to be helpful, because the space in front of the switches is the space we need.

The booking form asks for a repair preference. This is a preference and does not guarantee assignment to that table. Last month we called it a choice, and several people reasonably thought that meant the table had been reserved. We have changed the wording. If your preference is tied to an access need, reply to this message rather than relying on the form alone. We will confirm arrangements with you before the morning.

We have six aprons and expect eight people. You may bring an apron if you have one, but please do not buy one for this. We can rotate the two jobs that do not need aprons. The jobs needing aprons should still have them, which is the point of rotating the jobs rather than just deciding that two people can go without.

The kettle is now on the small table beside the window. The old table is needed for drying repaired items, so tea should be made at the new table even if the old one feels like where tea belongs. We finish at noon. Staying afterwards is optional, and packing up will be part of the scheduled morning rather than something that only the people who can stay get to do.

assertions.text: Retains the 09:00 induction arrival, 09:15 returning-volunteer arrival, safety reason for the quiet interval, and request that returning volunteers avoid arriving early.
Preserves the difference between a repair preference and a reservation, including separate contact and prior confirmation for access needs.
Keeps the six-apron/eight-person arrangement safe through job rotation, without asking anyone to buy an apron or perform apron-requiring work without one.
Retains the kettle relocation, drying-table purpose, noon finish, optional staying afterwards, and scheduled packing-up time.
Adopts the sample's direct, warm, lightly amused voice without copying its rain, sign-in-sheet, pen, or Saturday facts.
Makes the explanation less circular while preserving the practical reasons for arrangements and allowing restrained humor.

cases.task:
Revise this synthetic results-and-interpretation passage for a transport operations report. Improve the argument across paragraphs while preserving the design, exact observations, and limits of inference. Use only the evidence supplied here and do not add citations.

Source to revise:
We tested whether reserving the first loading bay for short-stay deliveries could make the morning schedule less unpredictable. The practical difficulty was not only that vehicles sometimes waited, but that a dispatcher could not tell which late departure would consume the recovery time built into the next round. The intervention was therefore aimed at reliability, although the measure we recorded was waiting time before loading rather than lateness on the next round. These are related operational concerns, but the second was not measured.

The study comprised 24 depot-days at one depot, with 12 under the ordinary allocation and 12 under the reserved-bay rule. Ordinary allocation was used in the first two weeks and the reserved-bay rule in the next two. Each depot-day contributed its median waiting time, and the reported condition summary is the median of those 12 daily medians. It was 9 minutes under ordinary allocation and 6 minutes under the reserved-bay rule. These figures are not medians pooled across all deliveries. The number of deliveries per day ranged from 18 to 43, so a pooled summary would give busy days more weight.

The fraction of deliveries waiting more than 20 minutes, pooled within each condition, was 31 of 360 under ordinary allocation and 19 of 348 under the reserved-bay rule. Two days in the first condition included a road closure. No days in the second condition did. We did not remove the closure days, since disruptions are part of the service being scheduled, but retaining them does not make the conditions comparable.
