The lower waiting times are compatible with a benefit from reservation and with differences between the periods.

A dispatcher recorded that the rule was easier to explain to drivers. This comment was volunteered in the final debrief and was not a scored usability measure. We include it because a rule that can be explained is useful in practice, not because the comment independently verifies the waiting-time result. The next test should alternate the rule across comparable days and record departure lateness on subsequent rounds. At present, the data support trying that test. They do not establish the reliability improvement that motivated the trial, even though the measured waiting times moved in the intended direction.

assertions.text: Preserves the one-depot sequential-period design, 24 depot-days split evenly, and daily delivery range of 18 to 43.
Keeps the 9- versus 6-minute median-of-daily-medians summaries distinct from pooled delivery summaries and retains the exact 31/360 and 19/348 tail counts.
Retains the road-closure imbalance, the decision to retain those days, and the fact that subsequent-round lateness was not measured.
Organizes the passage around the relationship between the reliability goal, the waiting-time measurements, and the narrower conclusion actually supported.
Does not convert sequential observational differences or the single volunteered dispatcher comment into causal or independently measured usability evidence.
Consolidates repeated cautions where possible while keeping distinct limitations attached to the claims they qualify.
Presents alternating comparable days and recording subsequent-round lateness as proposed future work rather than completed evaluation.

cases.task:
Edit this synthetic educational-measurement discussion into a coherent manuscript passage. Preserve its actual contribution and uncertainty, including the difference between agreement and validity. The supplied study is the complete evidence base; do not supply references or additional results.

Source to revise:
A scoring guide can make teachers agree while leaving them jointly mistaken about what a response demonstrates. We revised the guide because disagreements in an initial review often concerned whether an explanation counted as reasoning or merely repeated the question. The revision supplied paired examples at that boundary. It did not add questions, change the maximum score of 20, or alter the construct the guide was intended to assess. Whether it succeeded in preserving that construct is a question about the revision, not something settled by our intention.

Eight teachers scored 48 short responses in two rounds. Every response received ratings from the same two teachers in both rounds, and each teacher scored 12 responses per round. In the first round they used the original guide. After a workshop they used the revised guide. They saw the same responses again, with response order changed, and they could not view their first-round scores. The interval was one week. Changing the order and hiding the earlier scores reduced direct copying opportunities, but neither procedure rules out memory of a response.

The number of responses whose two ratings differed by more than two points fell from 16 of 48 to 7 of 48. The mean of all 96 ratings was 12.4 in the first round and 12.8 in the second, reported to one decimal place. That increase is sometimes tempting to describe as better performance, although the pupils did not produce new responses between rounds. It is a change in scoring. We have no external criterion against which to decide whether either round's mean is closer to an appropriate value.

The narrower disagreement count suggests that the guide and workshop package may help teachers apply a shared boundary. Because the workshop and guide changed together, their contributions cannot be separated. The repeated responses further limit an interpretation in terms of what would happen with unfamiliar work. These concerns do not cancel the observed decrease in disagreement; they constrain its use. A further study would need fresh responses and an independent account of response quality. Until then, agreement is the observed result, consistency on new work is an open question, and validity has not been established by making the ratings more alike.

assertions.text: Preserves the eight-teacher, 48-response, two-rater design with the same pairs in both rounds, 12 responses per teacher per round, and a one-week interval.
Retains the exact disagreement counts, the 96-rating means reported to one decimal place, and the unchanged maximum score of 20.
Keeps the guide revision and workshop bundled and acknowledges repeated responses despite reordered presentation and hidden earlier scores.
Distinguishes an observed reduction in large scoring disagreements from pupil improvement, accuracy against an external criterion, and construct validity.
Explains why the boundary examples motivate the revision without treating the intended preservation of the construct as demonstrated.
Integrates the limitations into a connected interpretation rather than repeating generalized uncertainty or presenting a detached checklist.

cases.task:
Revise this synthetic audio-processing report passage for clear technical exposition. Keep the preference study, transcript audit, and timing measurement distinct, with their precise results and limitations. Do not invent statistical tests, citations, or an overall performance claim.

Source to revise:
We evaluated a denoising setting intended for spoken archive clips. A cleaner background was useful only if the setting preserved the words, so the evaluation considered listener preference and transcript changes separately. Preference alone was not our definition of success. We also timed the processing step because the archive team wants to audition settings interactively, although the present timing run does not represent a full editing session.

Twelve listeners each heard both versions of 30 clips and chose the denoised version, the original, or no preference for each clip. Version order was counterbalanced within the listening protocol. This produced 360 choices, not 360 independent listeners or clips. Across all choices, 214 favored the denoised version, 118 favored the original, and 28 expressed no preference. The 18 clips classified as noisy contributed 152, 50, and 14 choices in those categories. The 12 quieter clips contributed 62, 68, and 14. Thus the overall preference count conceals a different balance for the quieter subset.

A separate audit compared transcripts prepared from each version. Three of the 30 clips had at least one word transcribed differently, and all three were in the noisy subset. The audit counted clips with a difference, not the total number of changed words. A second auditor confirmed that the transcript pairs differed but did not determine which version better represented the recording. We therefore cannot label every difference an error introduced by denoising, nor can we treat a preference for the denoised clips as proof that their words were preserved.

On the same workstation, a separate run over 200 fixed audio frames gave a median processing time of 42 milliseconds per frame for the existing setting and 71 milliseconds for the new setting. These are processing times for the tested frames, with input loading excluded. We did not measure the interface delay experienced by editors. The evidence favors offering the new setting for audition on noisy material while retaining access to the original. It does not justify automatically replacing every clip, and it leaves the transcript differences to be resolved before the setting is used for a final archive render.

assertions.text: Preserves the 12-listener, 30-clip design and all overall and subset preference counts, including the no-preference category.
Retains the three affected clips, their membership in the noisy subset, and the audit's inability to determine which transcription is correct.
Keeps the 42- and 71-millisecond processing medians, the 200 fixed frames, the same-workstation condition, and excluded input-loading time.
Does not treat 360 repeated choices as 360 independent participants or imply universal preference from the aggregate when quieter clips differ.
Distinguishes perceived preference, fidelity of words, and processing time from each other and from measured interface responsiveness.
Makes the bounded recommendation and unresolved transcript audit legible without replacing the already appropriate technical register with slogans.

cases.task:
Rewrite this synthetic archaeological-recording discussion so its motivation, observations, and recommendation form a clear argument. Preserve the uncertainty about what the recording methods capture. Treat the supplied observations as exhaustive and add no citations or field results.

Source to revise:
The recording trial began with a backlog, so speed was the reason for trying the new form. What we wanted to avoid, however, was a faster route to a record that could not be interpreted later. The photo-led form requires a scaled overview and four mandatory fields. The drawing-led form uses the same four fields and a hand-drawn plan. Both allow free-text notes about relationships with adjacent deposits. Those optional notes are not part of the completeness check, which matters for what the check can tell us.

We used the drawing-led form for the first 18 contexts recorded in a trench and the photo-led form for the next 18. The later contexts were generally shallower. The same two recorders worked throughout, and either could ask the other for help. We did not record which person supplied that help. It is therefore a shared-work trial of consecutive context groups, not a balanced comparison of independent individual performance.

Two of the 18 photo-led records and six of the 18 drawing-led records omitted at least one mandatory field on first submission. Median recording times were 11 and 16 minutes, respectively. These times include the initial record and exclude later corrections. Seven photo-led records and 13 drawing-led records included an optional relationship note. A lower count of such notes could mean that fewer relationships were visible, that the form elicited less description, or both. There was no independent inventory of all relationships against which the notes could be checked.

The photo-led records were therefore more complete by the mandatory-field measure, while also containing fewer of the optional notes that might matter to later interpretation. Calling them simply more complete would make the measure stand in for the record. Calling them poorer records because there were fewer notes would make the opposite mistake. The backlog made this distinction easy to lose because saving five minutes was immediately useful and missing interpretive information, if any was missing, would become costly only later.

We propose continuing the photo-led form on a limited set of contexts while adding an explicit relationship prompt and tracking correction time. That proposal is not an evaluated improvement. The trial shows an association with faster initial recording and fewer mandatory omissions in these consecutive groups. It does not isolate a form effect or show that the resulting archive retains every relationship needed for interpretation.

assertions.text: Preserves the consecutive groups of 18, their order and depth difference, the same two recorders, and unlogged assistance.
Retains the exact mandatory-omission counts, optional-note counts, and 11- versus 16-minute medians with later correction time excluded.
Keeps both methods' shared mandatory fields, their different primary visual records, and the optional status of relationship notes.
Distinguishes mandatory-field completeness from interpretive completeness and avoids equating fewer optional notes with demonstrated information loss.
Connects the backlog motivation to the tradeoff in later interpretability without claiming the sequential trial isolates a causal form effect.
Labels the limited continuation, new relationship prompt, and correction-time tracking as proposals rather than tested outcomes.
Keeps the distinct design, measurement, and archival-interpretation limitations clear and connected to the relevant claims, allowing purposeful repetition where it aids understanding.

cases.task:
Revise this committee statement into a persuasive, connected argument in the speaker's practical first-person voice. Retain the policy being proposed, the strongest objection, and the limits of the evidence. You may reorder material, but do not turn the statement into a neutral options paper or invent reasons for participants' behavior.

Source to revise:
I want us to keep one place on each Saturday repair team available for someone who cannot book a month ahead. I also want us to stop calling this a remedy for every kind of unfairness in the rota, because it is a small change to one part of it. The proposal is to reserve one place until two days before the session, then release it to the general waiting list if nobody has requested it. People using that place would still need the induction required for their role. We would not be asking an untrained person to take over a safety task because a booking rule had made a space.

The current system opens all places four weeks ahead. In the last eight Saturdays, the rota was full within a day on six occasions. Five volunteers have told us that variable work shifts make that difficult. We did not ask everyone why they failed to book, and we do not know how many people tried and gave up. The five messages are enough to show that the problem exists for those people. They are not a count of everyone excluded by the current arrangement. I would rather say exactly that than make the number sound either overwhelming or too small to matter.

There is a sensible objection from the table leads. They need to know whether the team has the right mix of skills, and a name added late is not automatically useful just because the place is filled. We already distinguish general helpers from people cleared to supervise electrical repairs. The reserved place should normally be a general-helper place. If a particular Saturday requires that place for a supervisor and no other supervisor is booked, the table lead should be able to release it early for that role, recording the reason. This exception is about keeping the session workable. It should not become an unrecorded way to return to the old system.

Some people have said that this will punish the volunteers who reliably book early. They would have one fewer place to choose from during most of the booking window, and pretending otherwise would make the case weaker. Their early commitments help us plan. The question is whether every place needs that protection or whether we can accept a little less certainty in one place to let a different group participate. I think we can, provided the role exception is real and the late booking is confirmed rather than merely hoped for.

Confirmation needs an owner. Under this proposal, the coordinator would contact the selected volunteer two days before the session. If the person had not confirmed by noon the following day, the place would go to the waiting list. A reserved place without this step could become an empty chair that everyone assumed someone else was filling. This is not a prediction that people with variable shifts are less reliable. The same confirmation deadline would apply to anyone taking a newly offered place at that stage.

I suggest trying the arrangement for six Saturdays and recording whether the reserved place was used, released, or reassigned through the role exception, along with any unfilled places at opening time. We should also ask the table leads whether the mix of skills was adequate. Those records will not tell us whether every volunteer feels included, and I am not proposing a six-week verdict on fairness in general. They should tell us whether this limited change can operate without leaving the teams short. If it cannot, we should revise it. If it can, we will have a practical reason to keep an opening for people whose calendars do not settle four weeks ahead.

assertions.text: Preserves one reserved Saturday place, release two days before the session, role-specific induction, the coordinator's confirmation step, and the following-day noon deadline.
Retains the supervisor-coverage exception, its requirement to record a reason, and the normal use of the reserved place for a general helper.
Keeps the six-of-eight rapid-fill observation and five reports about variable shifts without treating them as a population estimate or evidence of lower reliability.
Sustains an affirmative case for the limited proposal while acknowledging that early bookers lose access to one place and leads need a workable skills mix.
Shows how the role exception and confirmation ownership answer operational objections without implying that all scheduling uncertainty can be removed.
Preserves the six-Saturday pilot and its proposed operational records, distinguishing them from a general test of fairness or universal inclusion.
Presents a coherent case in a practical first-person voice without erasing the speaker's judgments or multiplying defensive disclaimers; reordering is optional.

cases.task:
Revise this synthetic proposal to an archaeological collections committee into a persuasive, connected argument. Preserve the exact allocation, the strongest scientific objection, and the limited purpose of the pilot. Treat the supplied laboratory procedure and collection details as complete premises; do not add analytical findings, conservation rules, or assurances about future tests.

Source to revise:
I recommend sending twelve ceramic fragments for the powder analysis, one from each of the twelve storage boxes selected for this project, rather than the twenty-four requested by the analysis team. Each box contains three fragments, so the proposed pilot would leave twenty-four intact. The larger submission would take two from each box and leave twelve. All thirty-six meet the laboratory's minimum mass requirement. The smaller batch is therefore a choice about how much material to use now, not a way of excluding fragments the laboratory cannot process.

The laboratory has confirmed that twelve is an acceptable batch and that its setup charge would be the same for either submission. We should not sell the smaller batch as a saving on that charge. Under the proposed procedure, each submitted fragment would be photographed, assigned its existing catalogue identifier, and then ground completely. The photographs would document its visible surface before grinding. They would not preserve a surface that a later investigator could examine with a different instrument.

The analysis team's objection is substantial. Two fragments from each box would let them look for differences within a box, whereas one cannot. A box is a storage unit, not a guarantee that its contents came from a single vessel or shared a composition. My proposal deliberately leaves that question unresolved. The first batch should instead check whether the laboratory can return a usable measurement linked unambiguously to each submitted identifier. A successful return would support planning a larger comparison; it would not show that one fragment represents its box.

Selection also needs to be visible. For this pilot, the curator would choose the fragment with the least visible decoration in each box, recording the choice before dispatch. That protects the more visibly decorated surfaces for now, but it could select a different kind of material. Neither these boxes nor the fragments within them were sampled randomly. The report should describe the submitted material without estimating the composition of the whole collection.

The remaining fragments should stay intact until the committee reviews the returned measurements and the identifier check. This is a temporary hold, not a promise that later surface analysis will be more informative. No such analysis has been commissioned. After review, the team could request a second batch with a question that justifies consuming more material. I favour this sequence because the first submission can test a necessary part of the workflow while leaving us something real to decide about afterward.

assertions.text: Preserves twelve boxes with three eligible fragments each, the proposed one-per-box submission leaving twenty-four intact, and the alternative two-per-box submission leaving twelve.

Keeps the equal laboratory setup charge, the acceptable twelve-fragment batch, the catalogue identifiers and photographs, and complete grinding of submitted fragments; photographs do not preserve their physical surfaces.

Acknowledges that the larger submission permits a within-box comparison that the pilot cannot provide, and distinguishes a usable, correctly linked measurement from evidence that one fragment represents its box.
Retains curator selection by least visible decoration, recording before dispatch, nonrandom selection at both levels, and the resulting restriction against estimating collection-wide composition.

Sustains the recommendation for a temporary hold pending measurement and identifier review, without turning uncommissioned surface analysis into a promised benefit or a second batch into an approved commitment.

Makes the reasons for the smaller first submission and its costs understandable in connected, candid prose, while preserving the affirmative recommendation and allowing different effective paragraph arrangements.

cases.task:
Revise this short position statement for a teacher working group. Strengthen the connections between its reasons and recommendation while preserving its deliberately limited claim. Do not add research findings or change the proposed assessment policy.

Source to revise:
I support keeping the common end-of-unit quiz, but I do not support using it as the sole basis for the unit judgment. A common quiz gives us a shared set of questions to discuss. When classes use entirely different tasks, it is harder to know whether a difference in scores reflects the work pupils were asked to do. That is a reason to retain a common task, not a reason to assume that it captures everything taught in the unit.

The present quiz has ten short questions. Eight ask pupils to select an answer, and two ask for a brief explanation. The unit also asks pupils to compare two methods and defend a choice. Neither of the explanation questions requires that comparison. This is an observation about the current questions and our stated unit goals. It does not show that short questions are incapable of assessing reasoning, or that every longer assignment would assess it well.

My proposal is to keep the quiz and add one classroom comparison task to the evidence considered at the unit meeting. The comparison task would be completed during the ordinary lesson. Teachers would bring two anonymized examples and explain how they applied the shared criteria. I am not proposing a numerical formula for combining the task and quiz, because we have not agreed what the weights would mean.

The objection about workload deserves an answer. Discussing examples takes time, and a task embedded in a lesson still takes time to review. We can make room by replacing the current meeting segment in which every teacher reads out class averages. That change will not eliminate the work, but it redirects some existing time toward evidence the quiz does not currently provide. After one unit, we should check whether the examples helped us make judgments and whether the meeting remained manageable. Keeping a common reference point and broadening the evidence can be compatible if we are specific about the work each is meant to do.

assertions.text: Preserves the ten-question quiz composition and the specific absence of a required two-method comparison in its current explanation questions.
Retains the common quiz, one ordinary-lesson comparison task, two anonymized examples per teacher, shared criteria, and absence of a proposed numerical combination rule.
Keeps the proposed replacement of the class-average readout and the review after one unit.
Distinguishes criticism of the present quiz's coverage from a general claim that short questions cannot assess reasoning or longer tasks necessarily can.
Answers the workload objection honestly by identifying a partial reallocation of time rather than promising cost-free additional assessment.
Preserves the speaker's clear stance and readable professional voice, allowing already effective contrasts and sentences to remain.

cases.task:
Revise this transport board submission so the recommendation follows clearly from the competing service priorities. Keep its candid voice and exact proposal. Do not resolve the tradeoff by inventing passenger counts, budget capacity, or certainty about future demand.

Source to revise:
The last bus should leave the riverside stop at 22:20 on performance nights, and the printed timetable should say so. At present it leaves at 22:05 every night. Staff sometimes ask the driver to wait when a performance runs late, but the driver cannot promise a hold and passengers waiting farther along the route do not know whether the bus is late or has already gone. The proposal is a scheduled change on the six performance nights next month, not a standing instruction to wait for the audience.

The operator says a 22:20 departure can use the same vehicle and driver if the final layover is reduced by fifteen minutes. That is an operational possibility, not evidence that the change costs nothing in resilience. The layover is currently the only recovery time before the vehicle returns to the depot. On a delayed evening the return may therefore be later. We have not estimated how often that would happen. The operator has agreed to test the arrangement for those six nights, subject to publishing the changed times in advance.

The main objection is from passengers who board after the riverside stop and do not attend performances. Their last journey would also be fifteen minutes later. They are being asked to accept a worse time for them so that others have a more usable time, and this should be acknowledged instead of calling the change better for everyone. We do not have boarding counts that separate audience members from other passengers. The argument cannot rest on a claim that the audience is the larger group.

What we do know is that the venue's scheduled finish on these nights is 22:10, making the present last departure unusable for someone who stays to the advertised end. The later departure supplies ten scheduled minutes to reach the stop, although it does not cover every overrun or every person's walking time. The venue should display the departure prominently and say that the bus will leave at the published time.

I favor the six-night trial because it creates a service that can be planned around and replaces informal requests with a public arrangement. We should record departures, depot return times, and complaints from passengers along the route, then review them before adding more nights. Complaints will identify concerns, not measure the views of every passenger. If we proceed, we should defend the choice as a limited tradeoff and be willing to reverse it, rather than describing the timetable as though no one loses anything.

assertions.text: Preserves the six-night next-month trial, the change from 22:05 to 22:20, advance publication, and the rule that the bus leaves at the published time.
Keeps the same-vehicle-and-driver condition, fifteen-minute reduction of final layover, possible later depot return, and absence of an estimate of its frequency.
Retains the 22:10 scheduled performance finish and the limited ten-minute interval without promising that all overruns or walking needs are covered.
Acknowledges the adverse timing change for downstream passengers and does not justify it using an invented audience majority or a cost-free-service claim.
Connects the recommendation to advance planning and a public timetable while preserving the speaker's affirmative judgment about an acknowledged tradeoff.
Preserves the proposed departure, depot-return, and complaint records, their review before expansion, and the nonrepresentative nature of complaints.
Gives the full submission a clear line of reasoning without turning every qualification into a separate disclaimer or deleting consequential uncertainty.

cases.task:
Revise this proof for readers who know finite sums and completeness of Euclidean space. Explain the compressed steps and the purpose of the estimates in connected mathematical prose. Preserve the hypotheses and the quantitative conclusion; do not strengthen the convergence rate.

Source to revise:
An iterative audio reconstruction produces vectors x_0, x_1, ... in R^m, where m is a positive integer. Put d_k = ||x_{k+1} - x_k||_2. Suppose 0 <= rho < 1 and numbers eta_k >= 0 satisfy sum_{k=0}^infinity eta_k < infinity and
d_{k+1} <= rho d_k + eta_k
for every k >= 0. We claim that x_k converges to some x_* and that, for each n >= 0,
||x_* - x_n||_2 <= (d_n + sum_{k=n}^infinity eta_k)/(1-rho).

Fix N >= n and write S_{n,N} = sum_{k=n}^N d_k. Summing the recurrence for k = n, ..., N-1 gives
S_{n,N} - d_n <= rho(S_{n,N} - d_N) + sum_{k=n}^{N-1} eta_k.
Consequently,
(1-rho)S_{n,N} <= d_n - rho d_N + sum_{k=n}^{N-1} eta_k
<= d_n + sum_{k=n}^{N-1} eta_k.
For N = n, the sums over k = n, ..., N-1 are empty and the displayed relation still holds.

At n = 0 these bounds show that the nonnegative partial sums of the d_k are bounded. Thus sum d_k is finite and d_n tends to zero. For p > n, telescoping the vectors and using the triangle inequality gives
||x_p - x_n||_2 <= S_{n,p-1}
<= (d_n + sum_{k=n}^infinity eta_k)/(1-rho).
The right side tends to zero, uniformly in p > n. Completeness supplies x_*, and taking p to infinity gives the claimed estimate. This also covers rho = 0. No geometric decay of the tail of eta_k was assumed, so the estimate should not be described as a geometric convergence rate.

assertions.text: Preserves the Euclidean setting, nonnegative summable perturbations, recurrence for increments, and full range 0 <= rho < 1.
Retains the stated tail bound with d_n and the perturbation tail divided by 1-rho, without claiming a geometric rate from summability alone.
Explains the finite-sum rearrangement, including why the negative rho d_N term can be discarded.
Justifies bounded monotone partial sums, the implication d_n tends to zero, and vanishing perturbation tails before asserting the Cauchy property.
Uses telescoping, the triangle inequality, completeness, and passage to the limit in the correct order.
Handles empty sums at N = n and rho = 0 without dividing by rho or silently restricting the hypotheses.
Makes the purpose of the increment-sum estimate clear through connected prose and displayed derivations rather than replacing the proof with a result summary.

cases.task:
Complete the single marked justification gap and revise the surrounding proof for clarity. Keep the adaptive setting and the exact identity and bound. Use only the stated assumptions; do not assume independent rounds or replace the proof with a citation.

Source to revise:
Consider n rounds of volunteer task assignment on a finite probability space. Let F_0 subset F_1 subset ... subset F_n be the information available through each round, and let X_t be an F_t-measurable indicator of completion, for 1 <= t <= n. Assignments may depend on previous outcomes. Define p_t = E[X_t | F_{t-1}]. Let w_t be F_{t-1}-measurable with |w_t| <= 1. Define
D_t = w_t(X_t - p_t),     M_n = sum_{t=1}^n D_t.
The claim is
E[M_n^2] = sum_{t=1}^n E[w_t^2 p_t(1-p_t)] <= n/4.

Because X_t is an indicator,
E[(X_t-p_t)^2 | F_{t-1}]
= E[X_t^2 | F_{t-1}] - 2p_t E[X_t | F_{t-1}] + p_t^2
= p_t - 2p_t^2 + p_t^2
= p_t(1-p_t).
Taking expectations after multiplying by w_t^2 gives
E[D_t^2] = E[w_t^2 p_t(1-p_t)].
Expansion of the finite square yields
E[M_n^2] = sum_t E[D_t^2] + 2 sum_{s<t} E[D_s D_t].

[Justification gap: the cross terms are asserted to vanish, but this has not yet been shown for adaptive assignments.]

Once this gap is filled, the identity follows. Since 0 <= p_t <= 1 and |w_t| <= 1, every summand in the identity is at most 1/4. This gives the bound. When n = 0, define M_0 = 0 and both sums are empty. Probabilities p_t equal to zero or one need no separate division or limiting argument. The weights are chosen using earlier information; their measurability is part of the claim, not an optional convenience.

assertions.text: Preserves adaptive assignments, the filtration, indicator outcomes, predictable weights bounded in absolute value by one, and the finite probability space.
Retains both the exact second-moment identity with w_t squared and the n/4 bound, including n = 0.
Fills the marked cross-term gap by showing conditional centering and using earlier-term measurability with conditional expectation, rather than invoking independence.
Explains how the indicator identity and predictable weights justify the displayed conditional second-moment calculation.
Justifies the upper bound using p_t in [0,1] and the weight bound while covering probabilities zero and one without invalid division.
Develops the reason for expanding the square and removing cross terms in readable mathematical prose, keeping substantive derivation steps visible.
Does not extend the identity to weights chosen after observing X_t or turn the second-moment estimate into an unstated concentration result.

cases.task:
Rewrite this finite-counting proof to make the objects counted and the two counting arguments easy to follow. Preserve both exact formulas and the treatment of small sets. The archaeological setting is only an interpretation of the finite sets; add no empirical claims.

Source to revise:
Let U contain n distinct recorded fragments. A tentative sorting assigns each fragment to a labelled tray A, to a labelled tray B, or to neither. Thus A and B are disjoint subsets of U, either of which may be empty. All 3^n assignments are included. Write
C_n = sum_{A intersect B = empty} |A||B|,
Q_n = sum_{A intersect B = empty} (|A|-|B|)^2.
For n >= 2 we claim
C_n = n(n-1)3^{n-2},     Q_n = 2n3^{n-1}.

To obtain C_n, count records (A,B,a,b) with a in A and b in B. Fixing A,B gives |A||B| records. Fixing the ordered pair of distinct elements a,b gives 3^{n-2} assignments of the other elements. There are n(n-1) such ordered pairs, proving the first formula. The tray labels matter here.

For the second formula, first fix one element to be in A, and then fix two distinct ordered elements to be in A. These counts give
sum |A| = n3^{n-1},
sum |A|(|A|-1) = n(n-1)3^{n-2}.
The sums run over the same assignments as before. Therefore
sum |A|^2 = n3^{n-1} + n(n-1)3^{n-2}.
The same expression holds for B. Expanding the square and using the first formula yields
Q_n = 2[n3^{n-1} + n(n-1)3^{n-2}] - 2C_n
= 2n3^{n-1}.

For n = 0 the only assignment has two empty trays, so C_0 = Q_0 = 0. For n = 1 the three assignments have squared differences 1, 1, and 0, giving C_1 = 0 and Q_1 = 2. These cases are handled directly rather than by applying the argument that fixes two distinct elements.

assertions.text: Keeps labelled disjoint trays, the unassigned option, distinct fragments, empty trays, and the full set of 3^n assignments.
Retains both claimed formulas for n >= 2 and the explicit values at n = 0 and n = 1.
Explains the double count for C_n with ordered distinct elements and the three independent placement choices for every remaining element.
Shows why the first and second factorial-moment counts combine to give the sum of |A| squared and why symmetry supplies the B term.
Makes the cancellation in the expansion of Q_n explicit without identifying labelled tray assignments or using an unjustified independence claim.
Introduces each auxiliary count through its role in the calculation while preserving the proof's concise, concrete finite-set interpretation.

cases.task:
Revise this proof into a clear explanation of convergence of fitted scores under regularization. Supply the compressed algebra and epsilon reasoning where needed, but keep the theorem about fitted values for a fixed matrix and response. Do not add assumptions of full rank or claim convergence of a coefficient inverse.

Source to revise:
Let A be a real m by d matrix, with positive integers m,d, and let y in R^m be a fixed vector of educational scores. For lambda > 0 set
x_lambda = (A^T A + lambda I_d)^{-1} A^T y.
Let P be the orthogonal projection onto the column space of A. We claim A x_lambda tends to Py as lambda decreases to zero.

Suppose first that A has rank r > 0. Choose a reduced singular value decomposition
A = U Sigma V^T,
where the columns u_i of U and the columns v_i of V are orthonormal, and Sigma has positive diagonal entries sigma_i. Applying the inverse to these v_i gives
(A^T A + lambda I_d)^{-1}v_i = v_i/(sigma_i^2+lambda).
Also A^T y = sum_{i=1}^r sigma_i(u_i^T y)v_i. Hence
A x_lambda = sum_{i=1}^r [sigma_i^2/(sigma_i^2+lambda)](u_i^T y)u_i,
Py = sum_{i=1}^r (u_i^T y)u_i.
Writing sigma_min = min_i sigma_i, orthonormality gives
||A x_lambda-Py||_2^2
= sum_{i=1}^r [lambda/(sigma_i^2+lambda)]^2 (u_i^T y)^2
<= [lambda/(sigma_min^2+lambda)]^2 ||Py||_2^2.

This estimate implies the limit. If Py is nonzero, for epsilon > 0 one can choose delta = epsilon sigma_min^2/||Py||_2 and take 0 < lambda < delta. If Py is zero, the displayed expansion makes the error identically zero. If A has rank zero, then A = 0, x_lambda = 0, and P = 0, so the conclusion holds without defining sigma_min. The inverse defining x_lambda exists for every lambda > 0, since for nonzero z,
z^T(A^T A + lambda I_d)z = ||Az||_2^2 + lambda||z||_2^2 > 0.

assertions.text: Preserves the fixed real matrix and response, positive regularization parameter, ridge definition, projection target, and absence of a full-rank assumption.
Retains the exact singular-value error bound and scopes the conclusion to fitted values for the given A and y.
Justifies the inverse's existence and its action on the right singular vectors, making the fitted-value expansion mathematically supported without requiring a particular order of exposition.
Uses orthonormality correctly to obtain the squared-norm identity and the sigma_min bound.
Makes the epsilon argument explicit with the supplied delta or another valid choice, without dividing by zero in the other cases.
Handles rank zero and nonzero-rank Py = 0 separately and does not define a smallest positive singular value for the zero matrix.
Explains how regularization changes the fitted components and why the quantitative estimate proves the limit without burying the derivation in compressed instructions.

cases.task:
Read this archaeological field-note introduction as a careful copy editor. It has already been approved for tone and substance. Correct only genuine grammatical errors or ambiguities that obstruct understanding; if none are present, return it unchanged. Preserve the writer's voice, including the approved joke.

Source to revise:
A field notebook is allowed to be untidy. It is not allowed to be mysterious in ways that we could have prevented. Before leaving a context, check that the number on the page matches the number on the bag and that your sketch has an orientation mark. Your future self may remember the trench perfectly. The rest of us have not been issued that future self.

Keep observations separate from interpretations when you can. “Dark band against the north edge” records something another person may be able to recognize. “Burning event” proposes an explanation. Both belong in the notebook when relevant, but they do different jobs. If you change your interpretation, add a dated note rather than making the earlier one disappear. A change of mind can be part of the record.

This does not mean every sentence needs a warning label. Write what you saw, say where you are uncertain, and give enough context for someone else to understand the uncertainty. A question mark without a clear subject is rarely much help. If rain or poor light limited what you could see, record that condition alongside the observation it affected.

At the end of the day, photograph each completed page before the notebook leaves the site. The photographs are a backup, not a replacement for the notebook. Check that they are readable before deleting any blurred attempts. We are trying to preserve a record of the trench, not a small private exhibition of your thumb.

assertions.text: Preserves the checks linking page and bag numbers, sketch orientation, and dated additions when interpretations change.
Keeps observation distinct from interpretation without suggesting interpretations are forbidden or require proof before recording.
Retains end-of-day readable page photographs before the notebook leaves, their backup status, and checking before deleting blurred attempts.
Preserves the approved dry jokes and direct voice instead of formalizing them or treating humor as an error.
Respects the copy-edit-only scope and permits an unchanged return because the supplied passage has no intended grammatical defect or blocking ambiguity.
Keeps the distinction between documenting actual uncertainty and adding a warning to every sentence, including the specific role of viewing conditions.

cases.task:
Check this approved audio-engineering explanation for wording that would actually mislead its intended readers, who are experienced editors. Make only changes necessary to correct such wording. Preserve legitimate terminology and the explanatory contrasts. Return the passage unchanged if it is already accurate and clear within its stated setting.

Source to revise:
In this session, the side-chain signal tells the compressor when to reduce gain; it is not itself mixed into the output. We feed that side chain from the dialogue bus so the music can duck when speech is present. The routing is deliberate. Moving the dialogue into the music bus would change the mix, not merely change what the compressor listens to.

The attack and release settings shape how quickly gain reduction begins and recovers. They do not move the spoken words earlier or later on the timeline. A slow attack may let the beginning of a sound pass before substantial reduction occurs. Whether that is useful depends on what we want the music to do around the speech, so audition the transition rather than judging the setting from its number alone.

The detector in this setup is fed before the dialogue fader. Lowering that fader therefore changes the audible dialogue level without changing this detector feed. If the music now ducks more than the quieter dialogue seems to require, that behavior is consistent with the routing. It does not by itself show that the compressor has stopped responding correctly.

For the current review, leave the routing as it is and compare the two saved release settings at the same listening level. We are choosing which recovery sounds less distracting between phrases. This comparison does not test whether a different side-chain source would work better, and it should not be reported as such.

assertions.text: Preserves the configured separation between side-chain detection and the audible mix, including the dialogue-bus source and music ducking.
Retains the stated pre-fader detector feed and its consequence that changing the dialogue fader does not change that feed in this setup.
Keeps the review limited to the two saved release settings at the same listening level, with the routing unchanged.
Preserves useful terms such as side chain, attack, release, detector, and pre-fader rather than replacing them with less precise generic wording.
Keeps the legitimate distinctions between gain-envelope behavior and timeline placement, and between a release-setting comparison and a routing comparison.
Respects the already-approved passage and returns it unchanged or with only a defensible correction, without manufacturing a need for extensive revision.

cases.task:
Make one limited update to this volunteer notice: public opening has moved from 09:30 to 10:00. Update both references to public opening and keep every other arrangement, wording choice, and joke as written. Return the full updated notice.

Source to revise:
The repair room opens to the public at 09:30 this Saturday. Set-up volunteers should still arrive at 09:00, and table leads should collect the tool checklist from the desk when they arrive. Please use the side entrance before public opening so the queue at the front stays out of the trolley route.

Visitors can bring one item each for an initial assessment. That is not a promise that every item will be repaired on the day. Some repairs need parts we do not have, and some items will need a specialist. The welcome team can explain this without apologizing for the entire history of broken household objects. The short explanation on the desk is enough.

We have moved the tea tray to the shelf beside the window. Keep it there, even if a clear corner of a repair table looks inviting. Drinks and open equipment have different ambitions, and we would like them to pursue those ambitions separately. The water jug and clean cups will be ready before the room opens.

At 09:30, the welcome team should open the front doors and begin taking names. We stop accepting new items at 11:30 and finish repairs at noon. Packing away is part of the shift, which ends at 12:20. If you need to leave earlier, tell the coordinator before Friday evening so we can assign the final checks to someone else.

assertions.text: Updates both the stated public opening and the front-door opening instruction to 10:00.
Preserves the 09:00 set-up arrival, 11:30 intake cutoff, noon repair finish, 12:20 shift end, and Friday-evening notification deadline.
Keeps the side-entrance rule, one-item assessment policy, repair limitations, tea location, and pre-opening readiness of cups and water.
Honors the explicitly limited update by leaving other wording unchanged instead of performing a general copy edit.
Preserves the deliberate jokes about broken objects and drinks near equipment without polishing them away.
Does not infer that a later public opening shifts every other scheduled activity or creates a promise to finish all repairs.

cases.task:
Review this approved explanation of a small educational-measurement pilot for accidental repetition or unclear wording. Edit only if a change would improve meaning or readability. Preserve real caveats and the conversational professional voice; an unchanged passage is acceptable.

Source to revise:
We asked whether pupils would interpret the new instructions as intended before using the task to compare their answers. In this pilot, eight pupils read the instructions aloud and explained what they thought they were being asked to do. Six described both required steps. Two described the first step and noticed the second only when asked to read the final sentence again.

That finding gives us a reason to revise the placement of the second step. It does not tell us how often the problem would occur in a full class. Reading aloud and discussing the instructions with an adult are also different from encountering them during an ordinary lesson. Both limits matter: the group is small, and the situation changes how pupils attend to the text.

We have moved the second step into its own sentence beside the response box. This is a revision prompted by the pilot, not a tested improvement. We will check the new version with another small group before using it in the planned comparison. The check will concern pupils' understanding of the instructions, not whether their answers deserve higher scores.

For now, the pilot has done a useful, modest job. It exposed a plausible misunderstanding while there was still time to change the task. We can value that result without treating eight conversations as a prevalence estimate, and we can describe the revision without claiming to know that it has solved the problem.

assertions.text: Preserves the eight-pupil read-aloud design, the six who identified both steps, and the two who noticed the second step after a rereading prompt.
Retains the completed text relocation, the untested status of that revision, and the planned further small-group check before the comparison.
Keeps the separate limitations from sample size and the interactive read-aloud setting rather than collapsing them into a vague disclaimer.
Distinguishes comprehension of instructions from answer quality and a plausible misunderstanding from a population prevalence estimate.
Allows purposeful reinforcement of the limited conclusion to remain where it aids understanding rather than automatically treating recurring caveats as redundancy.
Maintains the conversational, modestly positive voice and permits leaving the already-good passage unchanged.
